passages.title: The red bus
passages.text: The red bus stops at the end of this busy street.

passages.title: A cup of tea
passages.text: Could I have a cup of tea with milk, please?

passages.title: Lost keys
passages.text: I think I left my keys in the kitchen.

passages.title: Bad back
passages.text: My dad has a bad back, so he can't run.

passages.title: Shopping list
passages.text: We need bread, eggs and a big bag of apples.

passages.title: Good book
passages.text: She put the good book back on the wooden shelf.

passages.title: Wet dog
passages.text: The wet dog jumped into the pond and swam off.

passages.title: Sunday lunch
passages.text: My mum cooks a lovely lunch for us on Sundays.

passages.title: Thick jumper
passages.text: It is cold, so pack a thick jumper and a hat.

passages.title: Quick question
passages.text: Can I ask you a quick question about the test?

passages.title: Black cat
passages.text: A black cat sat on the mat and had a nap.

passages.title: Next stop
passages.text: Please get off the train at the next stop.

passages.title: Hot dog
passages.text: Tom got a hot dog and a box of chips.

passages.title: Lunch box
passages.text: Did you remember to bring your lunch box from the van?

passages.title: Football
passages.text: The children kicked the football up the hill.

passages.title: Wrong bag
passages.text: Sorry, I think you have picked up the wrong bag.

passages.title: Little shop
passages.text: There is a little shop just round the corner.

passages.title: Rest
passages.text: Let's sit on this bench and rest for ten minutes.

passages.title: Pens and pencils
passages.text: Ben lent his friend six pens and a pencil.

passages.title: Muddy boots
passages.text: Put your muddy boots by the back door, not on the rug.

passages.title: Morning routine
passages.text: I wake up at seven thirty every Thursday. Then I brush my teeth, have a bath and think about the things I need to do that day.

passages.title: The school run
passages.text: My brother walks the twins to school on weekdays. They always ask for sweets on the way. He says no, but they still ask every morning.

passages.title: Breakfast together
passages.text: Both of my children like toast with jam. My husband prefers porridge with honey. I only drink coffee, because I rarely feel hungry before nine o'clock.

passages.title: Catching the train
passages.text: I missed the train this morning, so I waited thirty minutes for the next one. I finally arrived at the office and thanked my boss for waiting.

passages.title: Washing up
passages.text: After dinner, my father washes the dishes and my mother dries them. I put them back in the cupboards. Then we all sit together and watch the news.

passages.title: Gym on Thursdays
passages.text: On Thursdays I go to the gym with three friends. We stretch, lift weights and run on the machines. Afterwards we feel tired but healthy.

passages.title: Weekly shop
passages.text: On Saturdays we do the weekly shop. We buy fruit, vegetables, cheese and cereal. My daughter always asks for crisps, and sometimes I let her choose them.

passages.title: Walking the dog
passages.text: Every evening I walk the dog along the path by the river. She sniffs the grass and chases the birds. Then we both head home for supper.

passages.title: Working from home
passages.text: On Mondays I work from home. I check my emails, join three short meetings and then think through the month ahead. It is quieter than the office.

passages.title: Laundry day
passages.text: Sunday is laundry day in our flat. We sort the clothes, wash the towels and hang the shirts by the window. By the evening everything smells fresh.

passages.title: The birthday card
passages.text: It was my mother's birthday on the thirteenth. I wrote a thoughtful card, wrapped a small gift and posted both of them on Thursday morning.

passages.title: Bedtime
passages.text: At bedtime, my son chooses a book and climbs into bed. I read three or four pages. He usually falls asleep before the end of the story.

passages.title: Packed lunches
passages.text: Every night I make packed lunches for the next day. There are sandwiches, apples and something sweet. My youngest says that the crusts taste strange, so I cut them off.

passages.title: The commute
passages.text: My commute takes forty minutes. I cycle to the station, lock my bike and catch the fast train. On the way, I listen to podcasts or the radio.

passages.title: Feeding the birds
passages.text: My grandfather feeds the birds in his garden each morning. He throws seeds on the path and fills the feeder. He says that thrushes are his favourites.

passages.title: Tidying the kitchen
passages.text: Before breakfast, I clear the table and wipe the surfaces. Then I empty the dishwasher, sweep the floor and take out the rubbish. It only takes ten minutes.

passages.title: Evening class
passages.text: Every Wednesday evening I attend a Spanish class at the local college. We practise verbs, learn new words and chat with each other. It's hard, but I enjoy it.

passages.title: Lunch break
passages.text: At lunchtime I leave my desk and walk around the park. I eat my sandwiches on a bench and think about anything except work. It helps me relax.

passages.title: Saturday chores
passages.text: On Saturday mornings my sisters and I share the chores. One of us cleans the bathroom, another hoovers the stairs and the third changes the beds.

passages.title: Running late
passages.text: I overslept this morning, so I rushed through everything. I skipped breakfast, grabbed my things and jumped on the bus. Thankfully, I arrived just in time.

passages.title: A walk in the park
passages.text: Last March, Martha took her dog for a long walk in the park. The grass was wet and the sky was dark, but they walked for hours. They passed a small farm, a stone bridge and a garden full of roses. When they got home, Martha ran a warm bath and made a large pot of tea.

passages.title: Email to a landlord
passages.text: Dear Mark, I'm writing about the flat on Church Road. The heating in the bedroom has stopped working, and the bathroom door won't close properly. Could you send someone to look at them before the weekend? I'm usually at home after four o'clock. I'd be grateful for a quick answer. Many thanks, Laura.

passages.title: The lost scarf
passages.text: On her first day at work, Kirsty lost her favourite scarf. She searched the car park, the corridor and the staff room, but it wasn't there. Later that afternoon, a porter knocked on her door. He was holding the scarf and smiling. He had found it under a chair in the waiting area.

passages.title: Booking a table
passages.text: Hi Paula, could you book a table for four on Thursday evening? Somewhere near the harbour would be perfect, if possible. Tom prefers seafood, but I'm happy with anything. I should finish work at about half past six, so let's say seven. Call me if there's a problem. See you soon, George.

passages.title: The market
passages.text: Every Saturday morning, the market in our town is crowded. Farmers sell carrots, cheese and fresh bread from their carts. There's a stall with hot chestnuts and another with handmade cards. My daughter always wants to stop at the flower stall, and she normally talks me into buying a bunch of daffodils for our hall.

passages.title: First driving lesson
passages.text: My first driving lesson was a disaster. I turned left instead of right, forgot to start the car properly and nearly hit a parked van. My teacher stayed calm and smiled the whole time. By the end of the hour, I could start, steer and stop. I'm learning again next Thursday afternoon.

passages.title: An apology
passages.text: Dear Mrs Morgan, I'm sorry I missed our meeting this morning. My train was cancelled because of a fault, and the next one was nearly an hour late. I should have called you earlier, and I apologise for that. Are you free on Thursday or Friday afternoon instead? I can come to your office at any time. Best wishes, Sean.

passages.title: The surprise party
passages.text: For her fortieth birthday, we planned a surprise party for Charlotte. We hid in the dark garden and waited quietly. When she opened the gate, everyone shouted and the lights came on. She laughed so hard that she nearly cried. Later, we danced on the lawn until after midnight, and nobody wanted to go home.

passages.title: Caught in the storm
passages.text: We were halfway up the mountain when the storm started. The wind roared, the rain poured down and the path turned to mud. We sheltered behind a large rock and waited. After an hour, the sky cleared, and we saw the whole valley below us. It was worth the walk, but we were soaked.

passages.title: A note to a neighbour
passages.text: Hello, I'm Clare from number fourteen. I'll be away for the next four weeks, starting on Tuesday. Would you mind watering the plants in my front garden twice a week? The spare key is with the porter downstairs. I'll bring you back something nice from my trip. Thank you so much, and see you in March.

passages.title: The art class
passages.text: On Thursday nights, Arthur goes to an art class in the old church hall. The teacher, a cheerful woman called Pearl, shows them how to draw faces and hands. Arthur's first portrait looked rather strange, but his work is getting better. Last week he painted a large picture of his garden, and everyone admired it.

passages.title: Lost at the airport
passages.text: When I landed in Bristol, my suitcase didn't arrive. I waited at the carousel for nearly an hour, but it never appeared. Finally, I reported it at the desk, and a kind woman wrote down my address. Two days later, a courier brought it to my door. Nothing was missing, though my shirts were badly creased.

passages.title: The new job
passages.text: Dear Grandma, I started my new job on Monday. The office is in a tall glass tower near the river, and I can see the bridge from my desk. My colleagues are friendly, and my boss seems fair. The work is hard, but I'm learning fast. I'll call you on Sunday afternoon and tell you more. Lots of love, June.

passages.title: Borrowing the car
passages.text: Hi Bart, could I borrow your car this Saturday? I need to take some boxes to my sister's new flat, and they're far too large for the bus. I'll fill the tank and park it outside your door by four. If it's a problem, just tell me and I'll ask somebody else. Thanks a lot, Carl.

passages.title: The fox in the yard
passages.text: Late one night, I heard a strange noise in the back yard. I looked out of the window and saw a fox in the moonlight. It was ripping open a rubbish bag and searching for scraps. When I opened the door, it stared at me for a moment, then jumped over the wall and disappeared into the dark.

passages.title: A thank-you email
passages.text: Dear Martin, thank you for the wonderful dinner on Saturday. The food was perfect, and your garden looked beautiful under the stars. I especially loved the lemon tart; you must send me the recipe. It was lovely to meet your daughter at last, too. We'd love to have you both round to ours next month. Warm regards, Barbara.

passages.title: The early bird
passages.text: My neighbour Bernard gets up before dawn every morning. By half past five, he's already out in the garden with a cup of coffee, feeding the birds. He says that the early hours are the calmest part of the day. I've tried it a few times, but I always end up falling asleep on the sofa by lunch.

passages.title: Return to sender
passages.text: Hello, I'm returning the shoes I ordered last Tuesday. They're far too small, and the colour is darker than in the photo. I've put them back in the box with the receipt and the form. Please could you send me a larger pair? If you don't have one, I'd prefer a full refund. Kind regards, Ruth.

passages.title: A day at the seaside
passages.text: In August, we drove to the seaside for the day. The beach was packed, so we walked along the harbour wall to a quieter part. The children built a sandcastle and searched the rocks for crabs. We bought chips and sat on the warm sand, watching the boats. By dark, everyone was sunburnt but happy.

passages.title: The broken heater
passages.text: It was the coldest morning of the year, and the heater in our office broke. By nine o'clock, everyone was wearing coats, scarves and gloves at their desks. Our manager ordered a large pot of soup for lunch and promised that the engineer would arrive before four. He finally turned up at half past, and we all cheered.

passages.title: New library opens
passages.text: A new library has opened in the centre of Fairfield after two years of building work. The council spent four million pounds on the project, which includes a children's area, a cafe and twenty computers for the public. Local residents were invited to the opening on Saturday morning, and hundreds of families came to explore the shelves. The head librarian said that the building was designed to be a place for everyone, not just for readers. It will be open from nine until eight on weekdays, and until five at the weekend.

passages.title: Staff meeting notes
passages.text: Thank you all for coming to this morning's meeting. There are three items to discuss. First, the office will be closed on the twenty-third of December for maintenance, so please plan to work from home that day. Second, we're looking for volunteers to organise the summer party. If you're interested, send an email to Rachel by the end of the week. Finally, a reminder that expense forms must be submitted before the last Friday of the month. Late forms can't be processed until the following month, which causes problems for the finance team.

passages.title: Rail delays
passages.text: Passengers travelling between London and Brighton faced long delays on Monday after a signal failure near Croydon. Several trains were cancelled, and others were held at stations for up to an hour. A spokesperson for the rail company apologised to customers and said that engineers had worked through the night to repair the fault. Services returned to normal by the afternoon. Passengers whose journeys were delayed by more than thirty minutes can apply for compensation on the company's website. The company has promised a full investigation into the cause of the problem.

passages.title: A new manager
passages.text: I'd like to introduce our new operations manager, Daniel Hughes. Daniel joins us from a large logistics firm in Manchester, where he managed a team of forty people for six years. He'll be responsible for improving our delivery times and reducing costs across the warehouse. Over the next few weeks, he'll be meeting each of you individually to learn about your role and to hear your ideas. Please make him welcome, and don't hesitate to ask him any questions. His office is on the second floor, next to the conference room.

passages.title: Weather warning
passages.text: The Met Office has issued a yellow weather warning for heavy rain across much of Wales and the south-west of England. Up to fifty millimetres of rain could fall in some areas over the next two days, with a risk of flooding in low-lying places. Drivers are advised to take extra care on the roads and to allow more time for their journeys. Some schools may close early on Thursday. Conditions are expected to improve by the weekend, although temperatures will remain lower than average for the time of year.

passages.title: Job advertisement
passages.text: We are looking for an enthusiastic sales assistant to join our friendly team in the town centre. The successful candidate will have excellent communication skills and a genuine interest in fashion. Previous experience in retail is an advantage but is not essential, as full training will be given. The role involves serving customers, managing stock and keeping the shop tidy. You will work thirty hours a week, including two Saturdays a month. To apply, please send your application form and a short covering letter to the store manager.

passages.title: School wins award
passages.text: A primary school in Leeds has won a national award for its work on the environment. Pupils at Oak Lane Primary planted more than two hundred trees, built a wildlife pond and started a recycling scheme for the whole community. The head teacher said she was extremely proud of the children and their parents. The judges described the project as an example for schools across the country. The prize includes five thousand pounds, which the school plans to spend on a vegetable garden and a new outdoor classroom.

passages.title: IT system update
passages.text: Please note that the company's computer system will be updated this Friday evening. The work will begin at six o'clock and should be finished by midnight. During this time, you won't be able to access your email or the shared drives. Before you leave on Friday, save all of your documents and log out of your computer, but leave it switched on. If you have any problems on Monday morning, contact the IT helpdesk as soon as possible. We apologise for any inconvenience and thank you for your patience.

passages.title: Cafe owner retires
passages.text: After forty years behind the counter, Margaret Allen has served her last cup of tea. The owner of the popular Corner Cafe on the High Street retired on Friday, and dozens of customers came to say goodbye. Many of them had been visiting the cafe since they were children. Margaret said that the best part of the job had been the conversations. Her nephew will take over the business next month, and he has promised to keep the menu exactly as it is, including her famous carrot cake.

passages.title: Fire drill
passages.text: There will be a fire drill at eleven o'clock on Wednesday morning. When the alarm sounds, please stop what you are doing and leave the building by the nearest exit. Don't use the lifts, and don't go back for your coat or bag. Gather in the car park at the front of the building and wait for your floor manager to check the list of names. The drill should take about fifteen minutes. If you have a disability that may affect your exit, please speak to the facilities team beforehand.

passages.title: Bus fares rise
passages.text: Bus fares across the region will rise by ten per cent from the first of April, the transport authority announced yesterday. A single journey in the city centre will cost two pounds twenty, compared with two pounds today. The authority said the increase was necessary because of rising fuel and staff costs. However, passengers' groups have criticised the decision, arguing that higher fares will push more people into their cars. Students and pensioners will continue to receive discounts, and weekly tickets will still be available at the current price until June.

passages.title: Quarterly results
passages.text: I'm pleased to report that our sales for the first quarter were twelve per cent higher than last year. Most of the growth came from our online shop, which has doubled its number of customers since January. However, costs have also risen, especially for transport and packaging, so our profits have grown more slowly. In the next quarter, we'll focus on reducing those costs and improving our service. I'd like to thank everyone in the team for their hard work, and especially the warehouse staff, who have coped with a very busy period.

passages.title: Festival returns
passages.text: The town's summer music festival will return in July after a break of three years. Organisers expect more than ten thousand visitors over the two days. The programme includes local bands, a jazz stage and a tent for families, with activities for children of all ages. Tickets go on sale next Monday and can be bought online or from the town hall. Residents living near the park have been asked for their views on parking and noise, and extra buses will run to and from the station on both evenings.

passages.title: Training day
passages.text: Next Tuesday, all customer service staff will attend a training day on handling complaints. The session will start at half past nine in the main meeting room and finish at four. A trainer from an external company will lead the morning, and the afternoon will be spent practising real situations in small groups. Lunch and refreshments will be provided. Please let your manager know as soon as possible if you can't attend, so that we can arrange a place for you on the next session in March.

passages.title: Hospital car park
passages.text: Visitors to the city hospital will no longer have to pay for parking from next month, health officials confirmed on Tuesday. The charges, which can reach ten pounds a day, have been criticised for years by patients and their families. The hospital will use money from its own budget to cover the cost of the change. A spokesperson said that nobody should have to worry about money when visiting a relative who is seriously ill. Staff will also be able to park for free, although spaces remain limited at busy times.

passages.title: Holiday policy
passages.text: I'm writing to remind everyone about our holiday policy. Each member of staff is entitled to twenty-five days of annual leave, plus bank holidays. Requests for more than one week of leave should be made at least a month in advance. Please check the team calendar before you book anything, as we need at least two people in the office at all times. Any leave that hasn't been used by the end of December can't be carried over to the next year, so do plan ahead.

passages.title: Cycle lanes
passages.text: The city council has approved a plan to build twelve miles of new cycle lanes over the next three years. The lanes will connect the main residential areas with the city centre, the university and the railway station. Supporters say the scheme will reduce traffic, cut pollution and encourage people to live more healthily. However, some shop owners are worried that the loss of parking spaces could affect their business. The first section of the route, along the river, is due to open next spring.

passages.title: Client visit
passages.text: Our biggest client is visiting the office on Thursday, so I'd like to go through the arrangements. They will arrive at ten and have a short tour of the building first. After that, we'll have a presentation in the boardroom, followed by lunch at the hotel across the road. Sophie will take notes, and Imran will prepare the figures for the new contract. Please make sure that the reception area is clean and tidy, and that the meeting room has enough chairs and a working projector.

passages.title: Village shop saved
passages.text: A village shop that was due to close has been saved by its customers. When the owners of the shop in Little Hampton announced they were retiring, residents decided to buy the business themselves. More than three hundred people bought shares, raising over eighty thousand pounds. Volunteers now help to run the shop, which sells bread, newspapers and local vegetables. The chair of the group said the shop was the heart of the village, and that losing it would have been a disaster for older residents.

passages.title: Recycling changes
passages.text: From the beginning of next month, the council is changing the way it collects household waste. Food waste will be collected every week in a small brown bin, while general rubbish will be collected every two weeks instead of weekly. Glass, paper and plastic can still be placed in the green recycling bin. Every home will receive a new bin and a leaflet explaining the changes. The council says the new system will save money and help the environment, but some residents are worried that bins will overflow in summer.

passages.title: Why we should walk more
passages.text: Most of us know that we ought to exercise more, but few of us actually do it. Gyms are expensive, and after a long day at work, an hour of running is the last thing anyone wants. I'd like to suggest a simpler answer: walk. Walking costs nothing, needs no special equipment and can easily be added to an ordinary day. Get off the bus a stop early. Take the stairs instead of the lift. Walk to the shops instead of driving. Each of these choices seems small on its own, but together they add up. Doctors say that thirty minutes of brisk walking a day can lower the risk of heart disease and improve our mood. Walking also gives us time to think, to notice our surroundings and to talk to the people we're with. It's an easy habit to start, and an even easier one to keep.

passages.title: Presenting our results
passages.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for coming. Over the next ten minutes, I'm going to talk you through the results of our customer survey. We asked over two thousand customers what they thought of our service, and I'm pleased to say that the response was largely positive. Eighty per cent of people said they were happy or very happy with their last order. However, there were two areas where we clearly need to improve. The first is delivery times, which many customers felt were too slow. The second is our website, which some people found confusing. In a moment, I'll show you some of the comments in more detail, and then I'll outline three changes that we're proposing for next year. There'll be time for questions at the end, so please make a note of anything you'd like to ask.

passages.title: In praise of libraries
passages.text: I've loved libraries ever since I was a child. Every Saturday, my mother took my brother and me to the little library at the end of our road, and we each came home with an armful of books. Today, many people think libraries are out of date. Why borrow a book when you can download one in seconds? But libraries offer much more than books. They are warm, quiet places where anyone can sit for as long as they like without spending a penny. They offer free internet access to people who can't afford it at home, and help to those who are looking for work. They run reading groups for older people and rhyme times for toddlers. In an age when almost everything costs money, the public library is one of the few places left that is open to all of us, and that is worth protecting.

passages.title: The four-day week
passages.text: Should companies move to a four-day working week? I believe they should, and the evidence is on my side. In recent trials, hundreds of firms let their staff work four days instead of five, with no loss of pay. Most of them reported that productivity stayed the same or even rose. Employees took fewer sick days, felt less stressed and were less likely to leave. Of course, this approach won't suit every business. Hospitals and shops need to be staffed every day, and some small firms might struggle to cover the extra hours. But for many office jobs, the long working week is simply a habit, not a necessity. If people can do the same amount of work in less time, why should they spend an extra day at their desks? A shorter week could give us all more time for our families, our friends and ourselves.

passages.title: Introducing a new product
passages.text: Thank you all for being here today. I'm delighted to introduce our latest product, a smart water bottle that helps you drink enough during the day. It looks like an ordinary bottle, but inside the lid is a small sensor that measures how much you've drunk. When you need to have a drink, the lid glows gently. It also connects to an app on your phone, so you can track your progress over a week or a month. We tested an early version with a group of office workers, and almost all of them said they drank more water as a result. Several also told us that they felt less tired in the afternoons. The bottle will be available in four colours from the end of April, at a price of twenty-five pounds. In a moment, I'll pass a few around so you can try one yourselves.

passages.title: Learning a language as an adult
passages.text: People often say that it's too late to learn a language after the age of thirty. I don't agree. It's true that children seem to pick up new languages without much effort, but adults have advantages of their own. We are better at planning, we understand grammar more easily, and we usually know exactly why we're learning. What adults lack is not ability but time and confidence. We're afraid of making mistakes and of sounding silly in front of others. My advice is to accept those mistakes as part of the process. Speak as often as you can, even if it's only for a few minutes a day. Listen to the radio, watch films with subtitles and talk to yourself in the kitchen. Progress will feel slow at first, but one day you'll realise that you understood a whole conversation, and that's a wonderful feeling.

passages.title: A case for trains
passages.text: Every summer, millions of us take short flights to cities that we could easily reach by train. I'd like to make the case for the railway. Flying looks quick on paper, but once you add the journey to the airport, the security queues and the wait for your luggage, the train is often just as fast. It's also far more comfortable. On a train, you can walk around, look out of the window and arrive in the centre of a city rather than an hour outside it. And then, of course, there's the environment. A train journey produces a fraction of the emissions of the same trip by air. Rail travel isn't perfect. Tickets can be expensive, and booking across borders can be confusing. But if governments invested in better connections and simpler fares, I think many more of us would leave the plane behind.

passages.title: Project update
passages.text: Let me give you a quick update on the new office project. As you know, we're moving to the building on Station Road in the autumn. The good news is that the builders are on schedule, and the main work on the ground floor is already finished. The kitchen and the meeting rooms will be completed by the end of next month. There is one problem, however. The new desks we ordered have been delayed by the supplier, and they may not arrive until two weeks after we move in. We're looking at two options. One is to keep our old desks for a few weeks. The other is to hire temporary furniture. I'll send round a short summary of the costs this afternoon, and I'd be grateful if team leaders could give me their views by Friday.

passages.title: Screens and children
passages.text: How much time should children spend in front of a screen? It's a question that worries almost every parent I know. On one hand, tablets and phones are part of modern life, and children need to learn how to use them. Many apps and programmes are genuinely educational, and video calls let grandparents talk to grandchildren who live far away. On the other hand, too much screen time can affect sleep, reduce physical activity and leave little room for imagination. I don't think strict rules are the answer. Instead, I'd encourage families to agree on simple habits together: no phones at the dinner table, no screens in bedrooms at night and plenty of time outdoors at the weekend. Children copy what they see, so perhaps the most important step is for us adults to put our own phones down a little more often.

passages.title: Welcome to new students
passages.text: Good morning, and welcome to your first day at the college. My name is Anne Edwards, and I'm the head of student services. Over the next few years, you'll learn a great deal, meet people from all over the world and, I hope, enjoy yourselves along the way. I'd like to mention a few things that will help you settle in. First, your timetable is available online, and you'll receive an email with your login details later today. Second, if you have any questions or problems, our office is on the ground floor of the main building, and it's open every weekday from nine until five. Finally, please look after each other. Starting somewhere new can be lonely, so say hello to the person next to you. Many of the friends you make this week will stay with you for the rest of your life.

passages.title: Against fast fashion
passages.text: The clothes we buy have never been cheaper, and we have never bought so many of them. The average person now buys far more clothing than twenty years ago, and keeps each item for half as long. This is called fast fashion, and it comes at a cost. Producing a single cotton shirt can use thousands of litres of water, and many cheap garments are thrown away after only a few wears. I'm not suggesting that we all stop shopping. But we could ask ourselves a few simple questions before we buy something new. Do I really need it? Will I wear it at least thirty times? Could I find it second-hand? Repairing a favourite jumper, swapping clothes with friends or buying from a charity shop are all small acts, but together they could make a real difference to the planet.

passages.title: Results of the staff survey
passages.text: I'd like to share the main findings from this year's staff survey. Over seven hundred of you took part, which is the highest number we've ever had, so thank you. Overall, satisfaction has risen slightly since last year. Most of you said you enjoy your work and feel supported by your managers. You also told us clearly what isn't working. Many people feel that internal communication is poor, and that decisions are often made without explanation. Others said that the office is too noisy to concentrate. We've listened, and we're making some changes. From next month, there'll be a short update from the leadership team every Monday, and we're creating two quiet rooms on the third floor. We'll run the survey again in six months to see whether these steps have made a real difference to you.

passages.title: Why I volunteer
passages.text: Every Saturday morning, I spend three hours at a food bank in our town. When I first started, I thought I'd simply be packing boxes and stacking shelves. I do plenty of that, but I've also learned a lot about my own community. The people who come to us aren't who you might expect. Many of them have jobs, some have young families, and most have never needed help before. A broken boiler, an unexpected bill or a reduction in working hours is often all it takes. What surprises me most is how much I get back. I've made good friends among the other volunteers, and I go home every week with a sense of purpose. If you have a few spare hours, I'd really encourage you to find out what's happening near you. Almost every town has an organisation that would welcome an extra pair of hands.

passages.title: Our plan for the high street
passages.text: Thank you for inviting me to speak this evening. Like many towns, ours has seen its high street struggle in recent years. Shops have closed, footfall has fallen and too many windows are empty. But I don't believe the high street is finished. I believe it needs to change. Our plan has three parts. First, we want to turn some empty shops into spaces for small businesses, artists and community groups, with low rents for the first two years. Second, we'll hold a market every Saturday, with local food and crafts. Third, we'll make the street greener and safer, with more trees, more benches and better lighting. None of this will happen overnight, and we'll need your help. But if we work together, I'm confident that our high street can become a place that people want to visit again.

passages.title: Reading for pleasure
passages.text: When was the last time you read a book purely for fun? For many adults, the honest answer is years ago. We read constantly, of course: emails, messages, news and endless posts on social media. But reading a novel is a different experience altogether. It asks us to slow down and to stay with one story for hours at a time. Research suggests that people who read fiction regularly are better at understanding how others feel. It also seems to reduce stress and to help us sleep. If you'd like to get back into reading, start small. Choose a book you actually want to read, not one you think you should. Keep it by your bed, and read ten pages each night instead of scrolling on your phone. Before long, you may find that those ten pages have become fifty.

passages.title: Safety briefing
passages.text: Before we start today's tour of the factory, I need to give you a short safety briefing. Please listen carefully, as it's important for everyone's safety. First of all, you must wear your helmet and your high-visibility jacket at all times on the factory floor. Keep to the walkways marked in yellow, and don't cross any of the red lines on the floor. Some of the machines are extremely loud, so ear protection is available if you'd like it. Please don't touch any equipment, even if it appears to be switched off. If you hear the alarm, follow me to the nearest exit and wait in the car park until we've checked that everyone is safe. The tour will last about an hour, and we'll finish in the canteen with tea and coffee. Are there any questions before we begin?

passages.title: Should homework be banned?
passages.text: Every evening, in homes across the country, children and parents argue about homework. Some people now say that homework should be banned altogether, at least in primary schools. I understand their point of view. Young children have already spent six hours at school, and they also need time to play, rest and be with their families. Studies suggest that homework does little to improve the results of younger pupils. But I don't think we should abolish it completely. A small amount of reading each night can build good habits and help parents see what their children are learning. The problem isn't homework itself but too much of it, set without a clear purpose. Instead of a ban, I'd like to see schools agree on short, meaningful tasks, and give children the rest of the evening to simply be children.

passages.title: Introducing the team
passages.text: Before we look at the figures, I'd like to introduce the team who made this project possible. On my left is Priya, our lead designer. Priya joined us last spring and has completely changed the way our products look and feel. Next to her is Owen, who manages our relationships with suppliers. Without Owen, we'd never have delivered on time, and he's saved us a great deal of money along the way. At the end is Grace, our newest member, who has been analysing customer feedback. It was Grace who noticed that our older customers were finding the app difficult to use, and her ideas have already made a big difference. I'm very proud of what this small team has achieved in a year. Now, I'll hand over to Priya, who'll take you through the new design.

passages.title: The value of boredom
passages.text: Nobody likes being bored. As soon as we have a spare moment, in a queue or on a bus, most of us reach for our phones. But I'd like to argue that boredom is good for us. When our minds have nothing to do, they begin to wander, and that is often when our best ideas arrive. Many writers and inventors say that their most creative thoughts came during long walks or quiet afternoons. Boredom also teaches children to entertain themselves. A child with nothing to do will eventually invent a game, build a den or draw a picture. If we fill every empty minute with entertainment, we never give our imagination the chance to work. So next time you're waiting for a train, try leaving your phone in your pocket. You might be surprised by what comes into your head.

passages.title: Closing a conference
passages.text: Well, we've reached the end of what has been an inspiring two days. I'd like to thank all of our speakers, who have shared so much knowledge and experience with us. I'd also like to thank the organising team, who have worked incredibly hard behind the scenes, and the hotel staff, who have looked after us so well. Most of all, thank you for taking part. The discussions in the sessions, and in the corridors between them, have been the best part of the event. Before you leave, please take five minutes to fill in the feedback form in your pack. Your comments really do help us plan next year's conference. The slides from all of the talks will be available on our website by Friday. Have a safe journey home, and I hope to see many of you again next year.

passages.title: The lighthouse keeper
passages.text: For thirty-one years, Edmund Hale had kept the light on Gull Rock, and in all that time he had never once let it go out. He knew every sound the old tower made: the groan of the iron stairs in a north wind, the tick of the glass as it cooled at dawn, the hollow knock of the sea against the rocks below. Visitors were rare. A supply boat came on the first Monday of each month, weather permitting, and once a summer a party of schoolchildren would climb the hundred and twelve steps and stare out at the grey water as though they expected to see America. Edmund liked the children. He liked their questions, which were always the same. Did he get lonely? What did he eat? Had he ever seen a shipwreck? He answered them patiently, in the slow, careful voice of a man who rarely spoke aloud. Yes, sometimes. Fish, mostly, and tinned peaches. And once, long ago, on a night he still dreamed about. But that story he kept for himself. When the boat left, he would stand on the gallery and wave until it disappeared, and then he would go back inside and polish the lamp.

passages.title: Betty's butter
passages.text: Betty bought a bit of butter, but she said the butter was bitter. If she put this bitter butter in her batter, it would make her batter bitter. So Betty bought a better bit of butter, and the better butter made her batter better. Try saying that three times quickly, and you'll soon discover why tongue-twisters are such good practice. They force your mouth to move between similar sounds at speed, and the moment you lose concentration, the words collapse into a muddle. Here is another to try. Six thick thistle sticks sat in a thin tin box by the thatched shed. Notice how your tongue has to dart forward between your teeth for "thick" and "thin", then pull back quickly for "sat" and "sticks". Now try a sentence that tests your vowels: a proud brown cow wandered round the town, then sat down on a mound and wouldn't be found. Don't worry if you stumble. Start slowly, say each word clearly, and only then build up speed. Within a week or two, you'll find that your speech in everyday conversations becomes clearer and more confident as well.

passages.title: IELTS: a place you like to visit
passages.text: I'd like to describe a place that I love to visit, which is a small fishing village on the coast of Cornwall. I first went there with my family when I was about ten years old, and I've been back almost every summer since then. The village sits at the bottom of a steep valley, and the narrow streets lead down towards a tiny harbour full of brightly painted boats. What I like most about it is the atmosphere. In the morning, you can watch the fishermen bringing in their catch, and in the evening, everyone gathers outside the pub to watch the sun go down over the sea. There's no traffic in the centre, so it feels very peaceful compared with the city where I live. I usually spend my days walking along the cliff paths, swimming in the cold water or simply reading on the beach. Of course, it does get crowded in August, and the weather can be unpredictable. But even on a grey, rainy day, I find it a calming place to be. For me, going there is a way of switching off completely from work and the pressures of everyday life.

passages.title: The letter
passages.text: The letter arrived on a Tuesday, which Clara would later think was fitting, since nothing important had ever happened to her on a Tuesday before. It lay on the mat among the bills and the leaflets, a thick cream envelope addressed in a hand she did not recognise. She carried it into the kitchen, put the kettle on and sat looking at it for a long time. Her name was written in full, with the middle name she never used, and the postmark was from a town she had never heard of. At last she slid a knife under the flap and drew out two sheets of heavy paper. The first was a short note from a solicitor. The second was a photograph of a house: tall and narrow, with a blue door and a garden full of roses. On the back, in faded pencil, someone had written: "For Clara, when she is ready." The kettle boiled and switched itself off, and she did not notice. She read the note three times, then turned the photograph over and over in her hands, as though the house might tell her who had been waiting all these years for her to be ready.

passages.title: IELTS: technology and work
passages.text: In many countries, technology has transformed the way people work. Tasks that once took hours, such as writing reports or finding information, can now be completed in minutes. Video calls have made it possible for colleagues in different continents to collaborate as if they were in the same room, and many employees can now work from home for at least part of the week. These changes have clear benefits. Workers save time and money on commuting, and companies can recruit talented people wherever they live. However, there are also significant drawbacks. Some people find it difficult to separate their work from their private life when their office is also their kitchen. Emails and messages arrive at all hours, and there is pressure to reply immediately. In addition, many routine jobs are disappearing as machines and software take them over, and workers in these roles may need to retrain. In my view, the effects of technology on work are largely positive, provided that governments and employers take steps to protect workers' wellbeing. Clear limits on working hours and investment in training would help to ensure that everyone shares in the benefits of these changes.

passages.title: The night train
passages.text: The night train left the city at a quarter to eleven, and by midnight the lights of the suburbs had given way to a darkness so complete that Tom could see nothing in the window but his own tired face. He had a compartment to himself: a narrow bunk, a folding table and a tiny sink that produced, after some persuasion, a thin stream of lukewarm water. He lay down fully dressed and listened to the rhythm of the wheels. Somewhere along the corridor a baby was crying, and further away a man was laughing at something on the radio. At about two o'clock the train stopped at a station whose name he could not read. A guard walked along the platform with a lamp, calling out softly in a language Tom did not understand. Then a whistle blew, the carriage jolted and the station slid away behind them. He must have slept after that, because the next thing he knew it was morning. Pale sunlight was falling across the blanket, and outside the window there were mountains, enormous and white, standing against a sky of the clearest blue he had ever seen.

passages.title: Red lorry, yellow lorry
passages.text: Actors and broadcasters have always used tongue-twisters to warm up before a performance, and you can use them in exactly the same way. One of the best known in Britain is "red lorry, yellow lorry". Say it once, slowly, and it seems easy. Say it five times, as fast as you can, and the first sounds of "red" and "lorry" begin to tangle together. The secret is to feel the difference in your mouth. For the start of "lorry", the tip of your tongue touches the ridge behind your top teeth. For the start of "red", it curls back slightly and doesn't touch anything at all. Here are a few more to practise. Willy's wheel wobbled while Wendy watched the wet weather. Fresh fried fish, fish fresh fried, fried fish fresh, fish fried fresh. Which wristwatches are Swiss wristwatches? The last one is famously difficult, because it switches between three similar sounds in quick succession. Don't be discouraged if you get them wrong at first. Even professional speakers trip over them. The aim is not perfection but control: the ability to keep each sound clear and distinct, even when you are speaking quickly and naturally in real conversation.

passages.title: IELTS: a person who influenced you
passages.text: I'm going to talk about my grandmother, who has probably had more influence on me than anyone else. She grew up on a farm in the countryside and left school at fourteen, but she was one of the wisest people I've ever known. When I was a child, I spent most of my school holidays at her house, and she taught me all sorts of practical things, like how to bake bread, how to grow vegetables and how to mend my own clothes. But the most important thing she taught me was patience. Whenever I got frustrated because something wasn't working, she would say, "Slow down. Do it properly, and do it once." It sounds simple, but I still think of those words whenever I'm under pressure at work or university. She also had an enormous curiosity about the world. Even in her eighties, she was reading books about history and science, and asking me to explain things I'd learned at school. She passed away three years ago, and I miss her a great deal. However, I feel that a lot of her is still with me, in the way I approach problems and in my belief that it's never too late to learn something new.

passages.title: The garden in winter
passages.text: In winter the garden belonged to the birds. The flower beds were bare and black, the lawn was stiff with frost, and the old apple tree stood in the corner like a man who had forgotten why he had come outside. But every morning, as soon as it was light, the birds arrived. First came the robin, who regarded the whole garden as his personal property and said so loudly from the top of the fence. Then the blackbirds, turning over the dead leaves with quick, impatient movements, and a pair of blue tits that hung upside down from the feeder like tiny acrobats. Margaret watched them from the kitchen window while she waited for the toast. She had never been especially interested in birds when her husband was alive. It had been his hobby, not hers: his binoculars, his notebooks, his long and to her quite tedious lists. Now she found that she knew most of their names, and that she looked forward to their arrival more than almost anything else in her day. She bought seed in large bags from the shop in the village and filled the feeder every evening, just as he always had, so that nobody would go hungry in the morning.

passages.title: IELTS: cities and the countryside
passages.text: It is often argued that young people should be encouraged to stay in the countryside rather than move to cities. While I understand the concerns behind this view, I believe that individuals should be free to live wherever they wish. There are certainly problems caused by the movement of young people to urban areas. Rural communities can lose their schools, shops and public transport as their populations age and shrink. Farms may struggle to find workers, and traditional ways of life can disappear. On the other hand, cities offer opportunities that the countryside often cannot match. Universities, hospitals and large employers tend to be concentrated in urban centres, and many careers are simply unavailable elsewhere. It would be unfair to ask a talented young engineer or doctor to give up their ambitions in order to keep a village alive. In my opinion, the best solution is not to discourage people from leaving, but to make rural areas more attractive places to live and work. Faster internet connections, affordable housing and better transport links would allow more people to work remotely from the countryside, and would give those who grew up there a genuine choice about where to build their futures.

passages.title: The storm
passages.text: The storm came in from the west just after four o'clock, and by five it was as dark as midnight. Rain hammered on the roof of the farmhouse and ran in rivers down the windows, and every few minutes the whole valley flashed white, followed by a crash of thunder that rattled the plates on the dresser. The children were thrilled. They sat at the kitchen table with their noses pressed against the glass, counting the seconds between the lightning and the thunder to see how far away the storm was. Their mother was less excited. Their father had gone up to the top field after lunch to check on the sheep, and he had not come back. At half past five she lit the lamps and made the children's tea. At six she put on her coat and boots and stood at the back door for a long time, looking up the hill into the rain. Then, just as she had made up her mind to go and look for him, a light appeared at the top of the lane, swinging from side to side, and a familiar voice called out across the yard, asking whether anyone had thought to put the kettle on.

passages.title: Sounds that slide
passages.text: When British people speak quickly, their words don't stay neatly separated. Sounds join together, change and sometimes disappear entirely, and learners who expect every word to be pronounced clearly are often confused. Take the phrase "what do you want to do". Spoken carefully, it has six distinct words. In rapid speech, it may sound more like a single long word, with the last sound of "what" almost silent and "want to" reduced to something like "wanna". The same thing happens in many common phrases. "Did you" and "would you" can each shrink to a single quick syllable, and "I don't know" may be little more than a rising and falling hum. These changes aren't lazy or careless. They are a natural part of fluent speech, and native speakers use them without thinking. Understanding them will help your listening enormously. You don't need to copy every shortcut in your own speech, but practising a few common ones, such as linking a final consonant to the next vowel in "an apple" or "turn it off", will make you sound smoother and more relaxed. Listen carefully to films, podcasts and conversations, and try to notice where the joins happen.

passages.title: IELTS: describe a celebration
passages.text: I'd like to describe my cousin's wedding, which took place last June in a small village in the north of England. It was a fairly traditional wedding, but it was also very relaxed and personal, which is why it was so memorable for me. The ceremony was held in an old stone church in the morning, and afterwards all the guests walked together across a field to a large marquee that had been set up on a farm. The weather was perfect, warm and sunny with a light breeze, so we spent most of the afternoon outside on the grass. The food was all from local producers, and there was a huge cake that my aunt had baked herself. What made the day special, I think, were the speeches. My cousin's father told some very funny stories about her childhood, and her new husband gave a speech that was so sincere that half the guests were in tears. In the evening there was a band, and everyone danced, from the youngest children to my grandfather, who's nearly ninety. I remember thinking that it was the happiest I'd ever seen my whole family together.

passages.title: The old bookshop
passages.text: The bookshop on Fenwick Lane had been closing down for as long as anyone could remember. A faded sign in the window promised that everything must go, but nothing ever did. Inside, books were piled on every surface: on the shelves, on the floor, on the stairs and even on the single armchair, so that customers had to stand while they read. The owner, Mr Pell, sat behind a counter at the back, half hidden by a wall of encyclopaedias, and rarely looked up. He seemed to regard customers as an interruption. If you asked him for a particular title, he would sigh, disappear among the shelves for ten minutes, and then return with a completely different book, which he would place in your hands without a word. The strange thing was that it was always exactly the right book. People went in looking for a cookery book and came out with a volume of poetry that changed them forever. They went in for a guide to Spain and came out with a novel about Russia that kept them awake all night. Nobody knew how he did it, and nobody dared to ask.

passages.title: IELTS: advertising and children
passages.text: Some people believe that advertising aimed at children should be banned. Others argue that such a ban would be unnecessary and unfair. In this essay, I will consider both views before giving my own opinion. Those who support a ban point out that young children cannot easily tell the difference between advertisements and ordinary programmes. They are therefore more likely to believe the claims that advertisers make and to put pressure on their parents to buy products they do not need, such as expensive toys or unhealthy snacks. Over time, this may encourage poor eating habits and an unhealthy focus on possessions. On the other hand, opponents of a ban argue that advertising pays for much of the content that children enjoy, and that removing it could reduce the quality of children's television. They also claim that parents, not governments, should decide what their children watch. In my view, a complete ban would be difficult to enforce, especially online. However, I believe there should be strict rules on advertising unhealthy food to young children, and that schools should teach pupils from an early age to think critically about the messages they see.

passages.title: Peter's pickled peppers
passages.text: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers. If Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers, where's the peck of pickled peppers Peter Piper picked? This old rhyme has been used to practise English for generations, and it is still one of the best exercises for the sound at the start of "pen". Hold your hand in front of your mouth as you say it, and you should feel a small puff of air on "Peter", "Piper" and "picked". That puff is called aspiration, and it is one of the things that makes this English sound different from the same letter in many other languages. If you feel nothing, "pen" may sound like "Ben" to a British listener. Now try a newer one that mixes the two sounds. A big black bug bit a big black bear, and the big black bear bled blood. Notice that there is no puff of air for "big" and "black", and that your voice starts before your lips open. Finally, a quick challenge for the end of your practice: please pass the plate of plump purple plums to Paula, but put the pears back in the paper bag. Say each one three times, getting a little faster each time.

passages.title: IELTS: the importance of sleep
passages.text: Sleep is one of the most important factors in our health, yet many people in modern societies do not get enough of it. Scientists recommend that adults sleep for between seven and nine hours a night, but surveys suggest that a large proportion of the population regularly sleeps for less than six. There are several reasons for this. Long working hours, stress and caring responsibilities all reduce the time available for rest. In addition, the widespread habit of using phones and tablets in the evening can make it harder to fall asleep, as the light from screens affects the body's natural rhythms. The consequences of poor sleep are serious. In the short term, tired people concentrate less effectively and are more likely to have accidents, both at work and on the roads. In the long term, a lack of sleep has been linked to heart disease, depression and other health problems. There are, however, some simple measures that individuals can take. Going to bed at the same time each night, avoiding caffeine in the afternoon and keeping screens out of the bedroom can all make a significant difference to the quality and length of our sleep.

passages.title: The interview
passages.text: Daniel arrived twenty minutes early and spent them walking up and down the street, rehearsing his answers under his breath. He had prepared for every question he could imagine. Why did he want the job? What were his strengths and weaknesses? Where did he see himself in five years? He had answers to all of them, polished and confident and only slightly untrue. At ten o'clock exactly he pushed open the glass door and gave his name to the receptionist, who smiled and asked him to wait. The waiting area was full of plants and very quiet. He sat on the edge of a leather sofa and tried not to look at the other candidate, a young woman in a dark suit who was reading a thick report as though she had nothing at all to worry about. Then a door opened, and a tall, grey-haired man came out and called his name. Daniel stood up too quickly, dropped his folder and watched his carefully printed notes spread across the floor. The man looked at the papers, then at Daniel, and laughed. "Don't worry," he said, kneeling down to help. "That's the most honest thing anyone's done in here all week."

passages.title: A walk along the canal
passages.text: On Sunday mornings, when the city is still half asleep, I like to walk along the canal. I join the towpath near the station, where the water is dark and still and the old warehouses have been turned into flats with balconies full of plants. For the first mile or so, there are joggers and cyclists and people walking dogs, and everyone nods or says good morning as they pass. Then the buildings thin out, and the canal runs between allotments and back gardens, and finally into open fields. Narrowboats are moored along the bank, painted in reds and greens and decorated with roses and castles, and smoke rises from their chimneys. Sometimes the owners are sitting on deck with a mug of tea, and if I stop to admire a boat, they're usually happy to chat. Herons stand in the shallows like grey statues, and once, just once, I saw the brilliant blue flash of a kingfisher. I usually turn back at the lock, where there's a little cafe that does the best bacon sandwiches I've ever eaten. By the time I get home, the city is awake and busy, but I carry a little of that quiet with me for the rest of the day.

passages.title: IELTS: learning online
passages.text: Online learning has grown enormously in recent years, and many people now believe that it will eventually replace traditional classrooms. I partly agree with this view, but I think face-to-face teaching will continue to play an important role. There are clear advantages to studying online. Learners can study at their own pace, at times that suit them, and from anywhere with an internet connection. This is particularly valuable for adults who are working or caring for families, and for people in remote areas who cannot easily travel to a college. Online courses are also often cheaper, and they give students access to teachers and materials from all over the world. However, online learning has limitations. Many students find it difficult to stay motivated without the structure of regular classes and the support of their classmates. Practical subjects, such as nursing, engineering or music, are hard to teach entirely through a screen. Perhaps most importantly, schools and universities are not only places where knowledge is passed on, but also communities where young people develop social skills and make lifelong friends. For these reasons, I believe the future lies in a combination of the two approaches rather than a complete shift to online study.

placement.title: A sunny morning
placement.text: The sun is up, so let's go for a quick jog.

placement.title: Dear Sarah
placement.text: Dear Sarah, thank you for the lovely card and the scarf you sent for my birthday. It was such a surprise. We had a quiet party in the garden, and my daughter baked a large chocolate cake. The weather was warm, so we stayed outside until it got dark. I hope we can meet in March when you're back from abroad. Love, Martha.

placement.title: Why breakfast matters
placement.text: Many of us skip breakfast because we're in a hurry, but I'd argue that it's the one meal we really shouldn't miss. After a long night without food, our bodies need energy to start the day. People who eat a good breakfast often find it easier to concentrate at work or school, and they're less likely to reach for unhealthy snacks later in the morning. It doesn't have to take long. A bowl of porridge, a piece of fruit or a slice of toast with an egg can all be prepared in a few minutes. If you really can't face food early in the day, try making something the night before and taking it with you. Overnight oats, for example, can be eaten on the train or at your desk. Small changes like this are easy to make, and after a week or two, you may notice that you feel more alert and less tired in the afternoons.
